name: Toggl Track
tagline: Track time quickly, edit entries, and report by project, client, and tag

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Up to 5 users; unlimited projects, clients, and time entries; 30 API requests/hour/user/organization; 1 connected Google or Outlook calendar account.

tiers.name: Starter
tiers.limits: Unlimited users; billable rates, project estimates, tasks, and reporting.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Unlimited users; approvals, labor-cost tracking, audits, and advanced project controls.
tiers.notes: First annual year is promoted at $14/user/month; regular annual renewal is $18/user/month.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom seats, security, support, and terms.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Up to 5 users; unlimited projects, clients, and time entries; 30 API requests/hour/user/organization; 1 connected Google or Outlook calendar account.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; Premium annual is $14/user/month for year 1 then $18/user/month; Enterprise custom
pricing.hiddenCosts: Every workspace member needs a license; vacant licenses remain billed until manually removed; added seats are prorated; refunds are generally limited to billing-system errors.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Toggl Track, track time quickly, edit entries, and report by project, client, and tag. The hard boundary is cross-platform apps, background tracking, integrations, team controls, and sync, plus ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow.
coreLoopDIY: Track time quickly, edit entries, report by project, client, and tag, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
requirements: optional accessibility permission for app-name tracking
whatYouLose: cross-platform apps, background tracking, integrations, team controls, and sync
moatNotes: ubiquitous capture, coaching, and team workflow
ongoingBurden: idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Toggl Track because the timer is simple, but people pay for frictionless capture and a history they trust enough to invoice or change habits from. The recurring cost buys idle detection, permissions, app metadata, privacy, notifications, sync, reports, integrations, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Kimai
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source time-tracking application with projects, reports, and exports.

alternatives.name: Clockify Free
alternatives.desc: Five users get timers, projects and PDF reports one month at a time; CSV, billable rates and approvals are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup; optional desktop, mobile, and browser apps
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects, clients, tags, users, and reports live in Clockify's cloud; exports are plan-dependent and the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: Free reporting is limited to one month and PDF export, while billable rates, approvals, invoicing, and richer controls are paid.

alternatives.name: Kimai
alternatives.desc: Timesheets, rates, reports and invoices are all there; approvals need its free plugin and the server still needs an adult.

facts.dataFormat: Users, projects, activities, rates, and timesheets live in MySQL or MariaDB; plugins, configuration, and generated files live in persistent server volumes.
facts.gapVsPaid: Kimai trades Toggl's polished hosted and native-app experience for a server, upgrades, backups, plugins, and ongoing administration.
facts.setupBlocker: A non-expert needs Docker, a domain and TLS, database and application secrets, email configuration, backups, upgrades, and optional plugins for some workflows.

alternatives.name: My Hours Free
alternatives.desc: A clean five-person timer with unlimited projects, clients and basic reports; approvals, rates and invoices are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup plus optional mobile app
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects, clients, tasks, and reports live in My Hours' cloud; the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: Billable rates, budgets, approvals, audit logs, invoices, scheduled reports, and richer exports are paid, making the free reporting layer thinner than Toggl.

alternatives.name: solidtime
alternatives.desc: Modern multi-user timers, clients and billable rates in one Compose stack; the desktop apps are still beta.

facts.install: Hosted signup, or Docker Compose with PostgreSQL and a reverse proxy
facts.dataFormat: Hosted records live in solidtime's cloud; self-hosted organizations, members, projects, clients, and entries live in PostgreSQL. Desktop activity capture stays local until the user converts it into a time entry.
facts.gapVsPaid: The hosted free plan is solo-only, and the unrestricted open-source path requires running PostgreSQL, a reverse proxy, mail, migrations, backups, and updates.
facts.setupBlocker: The hosted free plan is solo-only; self-hosting needs Docker, PostgreSQL, application keys, a reverse proxy and TLS, migrations, mail configuration, and optional Gotenberg for PDFs.

alternatives.name: Super Productivity
alternatives.desc: A local task timer with tags, reports and exports; collaboration is not the point.

facts.install: Desktop or mobile installer, or installable browser PWA
facts.dataFormat: Local web-app data lives in IndexedDB; desktop backups use local app storage, and optional synchronization can use WebDAV, Dropbox, or encrypted SuperSync rather than being required.
facts.gapVsPaid: It is a personal task timer rather than a client-time system, with no shared workspace, approvals, billable rates, client reporting, or invoicing.

alternatives.name: TimeCamp Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited people and projects get timers, auto-tracking and basic reports; app analytics, billable controls and approvals are paid.

facts.install: Hosted signup; optional desktop and mobile tracking apps
facts.dataFormat: Time entries, projects, users, activity records, and reports live in TimeCamp's cloud; its security page says production data uses AWS services and encrypted database storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan's reporting, export, billable controls, approvals, and invoicing are materially thinner, with free report export restricted to PDF.
facts.setupBlocker: The timer is clean, but automatic activity tracking needs a desktop agent and operating-system monitoring permissions.

alternatives.name: TimeTagger
alternatives.desc: A lean timeline, tags and PDF or CSV reports in one container; it is built for individuals, not payroll departments.

facts.install: Use the local web app, or self-host with pip or Docker Compose
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted instance persists records in its itemdb/SQLite-backed data store; exports include the project's VCSV format, TSV, and PDF.
facts.gapVsPaid: TimeTagger is designed around individual timelines and tags, not Toggl's collaborative clients, projects, billable rates, approvals, and team reporting.
facts.setupBlocker: Remote self-hosting needs Python or Docker, HTTPS, and manually generated bcrypt credentials; the local single-user web app is considerably easier.

alternatives.name: Traggo
alternatives.desc: A tiny tag-based timer with useful dashboards in one container; invoices and mobile apps never arrive.

facts.install: Single binary or one Docker container
facts.dataFormat: Users, tags, timers, and time spans live in a local SQLite database under the persistent Traggo data directory.
facts.gapVsPaid: Its tag-only model omits conventional clients and projects, invoices, approvals, native mobile apps, and the broader reporting workflow Toggl users expect.
facts.setupBlocker: The container is simple, but internet exposure still needs a reverse proxy and TLS, and the default administrator password must be changed immediately.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Starter plan and a personal desktop tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Toggl Track in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, SQLite, and optional OS accessibility APIs; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: track time quickly, edit entries, report by project, client, and tag, review patterns locally, and export a transparent activity record.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create one-click start and stop, manual entries, idle detection, tags, projects, and notes.
Keep any application-name tracking opt-in and never record window contents or keystrokes.
Add Pomodoro-style focus sessions, break reminders, and an optional allowlist blocker.
Provide daily, weekly, project, and category reports with editable corrections.
Export CSV and JSON and make the underlying event log inspectable.
Add automatic local backups and a privacy screen explaining every collected field.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out employee surveillance.
Deliberately leave out payroll and billing automation.
Deliberately leave out cross-device blocking and behavioral coaching services.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
